what: FirstCash Holdings runs pawn shops and a lease-to-own finance business. The pawn stores lend small amounts of money against jewellery, electronics and tools, and resell the items customers do not redeem. The finance arm, American First Finance, lets shoppers at furniture, tyre and electronics retailers pay over time.
customers: People without access to bank credit. Pawn customers need a few hundred dollars quickly and have an item to pledge; lease-to-own customers want a sofa or a set of tyres they cannot pay for at once.
money: Interest and fees on pawn loans plus profit on merchandise sold in the stores, mostly in the US and Latin America.
American First Finance: lease-to-own and retail finance at partner merchants.
moat: Scale in a fragmented trade. FirstCash operates roughly three thousand stores, far more than any rival, which gives it buying power, a bigger pool of merchandise and the ability to appraise items consistently. Licences are local and slow to obtain, which limits new entrants.
risks: Regulators have long been uneasy about high-cost consumer credit. Rules capping fees, in the US or in Mexico and Latin America, would hit the core economics directly.
The lease-to-own business carries credit risk the pawn business does not. If customers stop paying, losses land on FirstCash rather than being covered by pledged goods.
Latin American operations expose profits to peso and other currency swings.
Debt stands at about $2.6B against $125.2M of cash.
Only four analysts follow the stock, so the $247.50 average target rests on a very small sample.
opportunities: Pawn demand tends to rise when household budgets tighten, which makes the business counter-cyclical.
Gold prices feed directly into pawn collateral values and merchandise margins.
Revenue has grown every year shown, from $1.7B in 2021 to $3.7B in 2025, and trailing revenue is about $4.3B.
Free cash flow of roughly $605.6M against a $7.2B market value leaves room for buybacks and store additions.
watch: Credit losses in the lease-to-own arm. The pawn side is well understood and stable; the newer finance business is where a bad year would show up first, so the loss rate on that book is the number that decides how the whole company is valued.
